thread.title: Apple: Bears Cannot See The Forest For The Trees - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Boris Mikanikrezai
title: Apple: Bears Cannot See The Forest For The Trees - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Source: Tree and Forest , Drew Gaffney (Saatchi Art)
Apple under sharp selling pressure Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has sold off considerably since October, down around 33% from its all-time high of $233 per share on October 3. Still, Apple remains up a small 4% in the year to date, outperforming it FANG complex, as proxied by AdvisorShares New Tech and Media ETF ( FNG ).
Apple
Source: Trading View
FANG complex ( FNG )
Source: Trading View
Bears focus too much iPhone unit sales The weakness in Apple has intensified since the company announced in its November 1 quarterly earnings call that it would stop disclosing the number of units (iPhones, iPads, Macs) sold each quarter.
Apple CFO Luca Maestri justified this decision by highlighting the lack of correspondence between “the number of units sold in any 90-day period” and “the underlying strength of our business”.
By reducing the granularity of data, the Apple stock has priced a higher level of uncertainty, thereby negative for the stock. At the UBS tech conference earlier in November, which gathered three Apple experts, Ben Bajarin (Principal at Creative Strategies), Carolina Milanesi (Principal Analyst at Creative Strategies), and Mark Gruman (Consumer technology journalist at Bloomberg), everyone agreed that Apple would be more difficult to follow after the removal of unit disclosures.
Unsurprisingly, this comes at a time when units are either flat or down in all segments, which has led a number of investors to believe that Apple is maybe hiding its weak spots.
Time to focus on Apple’s big transformation However, the company’s decision is likely to have been carefully taken by the management ahead of the coming iPhone cycle. A key motive could be to change investor perception of the company’s business, from a traditional hardware company to a services and media company in which the hardware (iPhone or any other device) marks only the first step in Apple’s ecosystem.
If Apple is successful in doing so, Apple's multiple could increase significantly.
In this respect, RBC’s base case of $240 per share reflects a ~18x FY2019 EPS. According to RBC, the valuation multiple chosen is slightly higher than its historical level because the Services business, which becomes an incrementally larger part of the overall business, warrants a higher multiple due to its higher corporate margin and growth trajectory.
Source: RBC
While investors have focused on the slower-than-expected iPhone unit sales for Q4 (46.9 million units vs market expectations of 47.5 million units, according to Factse t), investors seem to have completely overlooked the double-digit growth in installed base.
According to JP Morgan, the growth is driven by:
1) new subscribers; 2) incremental consumer switching to iOS; and 3) replacement units from existing iOS users making it to the secondary market (we estimate Apple has a 50% share of the secondary market relative to 15% of new smartphone market).
JP Morgan estimates that the total installed base in 2017 reached 1.4bn devices (including ~1bn iPhones) and forecasts the total installed base at 1.9bn by 2021, corresponding to a growth of 7% CAGR.
Source: JPM
The growth in the installed base of Apple devises constitutes a major contributor to revenue growth in the Services business.
Services revenue, which totalled $30bn in 2017 (+26% year on year) and represented to 13% of total revenue, is likely to become increasingly large contributor to total revenue in the coming years. JPM estimates that 20% of total revenue ($68 billion) will be driven by Services by 2021, implying a growth in Services business of 23% CAGR from 2017 to 2021.
Services revenue is set to be an increasingly large contributor to total revenue growth. Between 2012 and 2017, Services revenue contributed by 20% ($17 billion) to total revenue growth ($73 billion) while iPhone sales contributed by 74% ($63 billion).
Source: JPM
Given the robust and steady growth in services revenue, total revenue growth should be increasingly driven by services revenues in the coming years.
The solid growth in installed base, which has been overlooked by most investors, is a tangible sign that Apple is set to move toward a services-driven company at a faster and stronger pace than the market is willing to realize.
Bottom line: The recent sell-off in Apple, based on a flawed view that what only matters to valuation is iPhone sales, constitutes an opportunity for long-term investors. This is only a matter of time before Apple becomes re-rated to reflect its rapid transformation toward a services and media company.
